identification.summary: Heart Typhoon is Microsoft's name for a China-origin actor that Microsoft maps to HELIUM, AURORA PANDA, APT17, Hidden Lynx, DeputyDog and other vendor names [S1]. MITRE describes APT17 as a China-based group that has conducted network intrusions against U.S. government entities, the defense industry, law firms, information technology companies, mining companies and non-government organizations [S2][S3]. Symantec described Hidden Lynx in 2013 as a professional team with advanced capabilities, responsible for compromising security firm Bit9's code-signing certificate as part of the larger VOHO watering-hole campaign [S4].
identification.firstObserved: Symantec: Hidden Lynx in operation since at least 2009, with affiliations to 'Operation Aurora' [S4]. FireEye's named APT17 report was published 2015-05-14 [S3].
identification.notes: Microsoft name: Heart Typhoon (legacy element name HELIUM); Microsoft also lists AURORA PANDA, APT17, Hidden Lynx, ATG3, Red Typhoon, KAOS, TG-8153, SportsFans, DeputyDog and Tailgater for this actor [S1]. MITRE tracks APT17 as G0025 with the alias Deputy Dog [S2]. The MISP galaxy APT17 entry also lists BRONZE KEYSTONE (Secureworks) and merges Axiom/Group 72 (MITRE G0001) into the same entry [S7]; Microsoft tracks Axiom-related names separately, so Axiom facts are not merged here. Note that Microsoft also lists KAOS under Leopard Typhoon [S1].

attribution.sponsor: People's Republic of China (suspected). The Council on Foreign Relations data in the MISP galaxy lists China as the suspected state sponsor [S7]. Symantec assessed Hidden Lynx as likely a 'hackers for hire' organization whose attacks on government contractors and the defense industry suggest it had been working for nation states, with much of its infrastructure and tooling originating from network infrastructure in China [S4].
attribution.confidence: Microsoft records the actor's origin as China in its naming mapping [S1]; no Microsoft confidence statement was located. MISP records an attribution-confidence value of 50 [S7]. No U.S. government indictment or advisory naming APT17/Heart Typhoon was located in the sources gathered.
attribution.basis: Vendor technical reporting: Symantec Hidden Lynx analysis of tooling, infrastructure and targeting [S4]; FireEye infrastructure links between DeputyDog and the Bit9 intrusion [S5]; FireEye APT17 report as summarized by MITRE [S2][S3]; Microsoft naming mapping [S1].

objectives: Espionage and theft of specific information for competitive advantage at corporate and nation-state level, according to Symantec, which judged it unlikely the group used stolen data for direct financial gain [S4]. Targeting of government contractors and the defense industry indicates pursuit of confidential information and advanced technology such as aerospace [S4]. Symantec also notes Microsoft's claim that the related Operation Aurora targeted databases of emails marked for court-ordered wiretaps, characterized as counter-intelligence [S4].

sectors: Defense industrial base and government contractors [S2][S4]
Financial services (investment banks, asset managers, stock exchanges) [S4]
Information technology and security vendors (e.g., Bit9) [S2][S4]
regions: CFR-listed suspected victims: Netherlands, Italy, United Kingdom, Belgium, Russia, Indonesia, Germany, Switzerland, China [S7]
targeting.notes: Symantec reported hundreds of organizations worldwide targeted since November 2011, with financial services the most heavily targeted industry [S4]. The VOHO watering hole predominantly targeted US organizations, including the Boston, Massachusetts area, and nearly 4,000 machines downloaded a payload [S4].

capabilities.summary: Symantec described two teams: one distributing Backdoor.Moudoor (a customized Gh0st RAT) for large-scale campaigns and one using Trojan.Naid against high-value targets; Backdoor.Hikit was installed on public-facing DMZ servers [S4]. The group used strategic web compromises (watering holes), spear-phishing, supply-chain compromise and trojanized software updates, and used three zero-day browser exploits between 2011 and 2013 (including CVE-2012-1875 and CVE-2012-1889) [S4]. It stole a code-signing certificate from Bit9 and signed 32 malicious files to defeat application whitelisting [S4]. FireEye tied the 2013 CVE-2013-3893 Internet Explorer zero-day campaign (DeputyDog) to the same actor that compromised Bit9 [S5]. MITRE, citing FireEye, reports that APT17 created and cultivated Microsoft TechNet profile pages and used them as C2 infrastructure, and lists BLACKCOFFEE malware [S2][S3].

campaigns.name: Operation Aurora affiliation
campaigns.summary: Symantec states Hidden Lynx has affiliations to Operation Aurora; Trojan.Naid was also found in Aurora.

campaigns.name: GOTHAM watering hole
campaigns.summary: First zero-day of 2012 (IE CVE-2012-1875) used via a compromised website.

campaigns.name: VOHO watering-hole campaign
campaigns.summary: Ten legitimate websites compromised; two phases from 25 June to 18 July 2012 using CVE-2012-1889 and then CVE-2012-1723; nearly 4,000 machines downloaded payloads, mostly in the US.

campaigns.name: Bit9 compromise
campaigns.summary: SQL injection against a Bit9 public-facing server, Hikit installed, code-signing certificate used to sign 32 malicious files; disclosed by Bit9 in February 2013; three Bit9 customers impacted.

campaigns.name: FINSHO campaign
campaigns.summary: Early use of Java CVE-2013-1493 against Japanese targets to deliver Moudoor and Naid.

campaigns.name: Operation DeputyDog
campaigns.summary: IE zero-day CVE-2013-3893 used against entities in Japan from as early as 19 August 2013; FireEye linked C2 infrastructure to the Bit9 attackers.

campaigns.name: TechNet C2 obfuscation exposed (BLACKCOFFEE)
campaigns.summary: FireEye report, titled as a FireEye and Microsoft exposure, describes APT17 using TechNet profile pages as C2 for BLACKCOFFEE.

campaigns.name: CCleaner supply-chain backdoor (contested attribution)
campaigns.summary: Intezer reported code overlap between the backdoor in CCleaner v5.33 and earlier APT17 samples, following a Kaspersky researcher's Axiom-umbrella link; this is a vendor code-similarity assessment, not confirmed attribution.

diamond.adversary: China-origin actor per Microsoft [S1]; assessed by Symantec as a 50 to 100 person professional hacker-for-hire organization likely tasked for nation-state ends [S4].
diamond.capability: Moudoor (Gh0st RAT variant), Naid, Hikit, BLACKCOFFEE; browser and Java zero-days; stolen code-signing certificates; supply-chain trojanization [S2][S4][S5].
diamond.infrastructure: Compromised legitimate websites used as watering holes [S4]; C2 hosts in Hong Kong and South Korea and actor-registered domains during DeputyDog [S5]; Microsoft TechNet profile pages abused for C2 [S2][S3].
diamond.victim: US government and defense contractors, financial services, IT and security vendors, law firms, mining and NGOs; Japanese and South Korean organizations [S2][S4][S5].
diamond.socioPolitical: Collection of corporate and nation-state information, including advanced technology, to close technological gaps and gain competitive advantage [S4].
diamond.technology: Trust in legitimate websites, signed binaries and application whitelisting, legitimate web services such as TechNet, and software update channels [S2][S4].

gaps: No Microsoft Threat Intelligence report describing Heart Typhoon activity was located; Microsoft's coverage here is limited to the naming mapping [S1].
The FireEye APT17 report (2015) could not be opened; its content is cited only through MITRE ATT&CK's summary [S2][S3].
Bit9's 2013 disclosure, RSA's 2012 VOHO paper, CFR, Recorded Future and Secureworks (BRONZE KEYSTONE) profiles could not be opened; facts about them come through Symantec [S4] and MISP [S7].
Intrusion Truth (2019) public claims linking APT17 to the MSS Jinan bureau could not be accessed and are not included; no government attribution of APT17 to a specific PRC organization was verified.

Cluster boundaries: MISP merges APT17 with Axiom/Group 72 (G0001) [S7], while Microsoft and MITRE track them separately. KAOS appears under both Heart Typhoon and Leopard Typhoon in Microsoft's mapping [S1]. Hidden Lynx, DeputyDog and APT17 are linked by vendor mapping, not by a single primary report.

The 2017 CCleaner attribution rests on code similarity; the Intezer post also contains an unsupported statement tying earlier attacks to PLA Unit 61398 (APT1), which conflicts with Symantec's distinction between Hidden Lynx and APT1 [S4][S6].
No public reporting after 2017 attributed to Heart Typhoon/APT17 was found in the sources gathered; current activity status is unknown. Web search budget was exhausted during this research run.

implications.jipoe: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. STEP 1 (OE): Key terrain includes websites frequented by defense, government and financial personnel, public-facing DMZ servers, code-signing infrastructure of security vendors, and software build/update channels [S4][S6]. STEP 2 (effects): Signed malware and abused legitimate services (TechNet) degrade the value of whitelisting and reputation-based defenses and blend C2 into trusted traffic [S2][S4]. STEP 3 (adversary template): strategic web compromise or supply-chain implant, browser or Java exploit, Naid/Moudoor/Hikit or BLACKCOFFEE implant, C2 via actor domains or legitimate web pages, targeted data theft [S2][S4][S5]. STEP 4: MLCOA is targeted espionage against defense contractors and government networks via watering holes on sector-specific websites [S4]. MDCOA is compromise of a trusted software vendor or code-signing chain to reach many DoD-adjacent networks at once [S4][S6]. Candidate indicators: unexpected binaries signed by security or software vendors; outbound HTTP on port 443 that is not TLS with unusual headers such as 'Agtid' [S5]; endpoints retrieving content from forum or profile pages followed by connections to newly decoded hosts [S2]; compromised sector websites serving exploits shortly after zero-day disclosures [S4].
implications.jcc2: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. (1) Situational awareness: track code-signing certificate revocations and vendor supply-chain incidents as mission-relevant events, since this actor used a stolen certificate to defeat whitelisting at defense-sector customers [S4]. (2) Authorities: watering-hole and supply-chain intrusions sit on civilian and vendor infrastructure outside DoD networks; response requires coordination with DC3, the DIB CS program and law enforcement rather than direct DoD action [S4]. (3) Mission assurance: rapid patching of browser and Java zero-days used against defense-industry visitors, and egress controls on DMZ servers that hosted Hikit [S4][S5]. (4) Coordination: share indicators with Microsoft and vendors when legitimate cloud or community services are abused for C2, as with TechNet [S2][S3].
